sentences: The best AI image generator on October 26, 2026 depends on the job, because four models now split the field and three of them are under seven weeks old.

OpenAI shipped ChatGPT Images 2.5 on September 8, Google released Nano Banana 2.1 on October 6, and Black Forest Labs followed on October 15 with FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6-billion-parameter open-weights model that anyone can download.
Midjourney’s V8.2, the oldest of the four, has been the default since July 24.

Midjourney starts at $10 a month with no official API, Nano Banana 2.1 charges a reported $0.0336 for a 1K image through the Gemini API, and Klein’s hosted tiers start at $0.008 for a 768 by 768 image.
OpenAI bills by the token, so a clean per-image number does not exist yet.
Google’s Nano Banana 2.1 launch and price cut also set a hard deadline: the older Nano Banana 2 is reported to shut down on October 29, three days from now.
OpenAI’s side moved just as fast.
The ChatGPT Images 2.5 rollout cut generation latency by up to 50% versus Images 2.0, according to OpenAI.
Each vendor now pitches the same things: sharper text, tighter editing, more reference images and lower cost.
The differences sit in access, licensing and who controls the weights.
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
No single model wins every task, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling a subscription.
The picks below come from the verified record as of today, and each one names the trade-off you accept.
Treat that list as a starting point.
The evidence behind each pick is uneven, and the cost of each choice changes once you scale past a few dozen images.
The image-model market reset between July 23 and October 26.
Black Forest Labs announced its FLUX 3 family on July 23.
Midjourney made V8.2 its default a day later.
OpenAI, Google and Black Forest Labs then released new image models inside a 37-day window.
Every dated event in the verified record fits in one table.
First, the vendors released into each other’s news cycles, so every launch claimed some form of leadership the same week.
Second, the most reliable evidence is thin for the newest products.
OpenAI’s release notes and the Black Forest Labs press release are primary documents.
Almost everything else on Nano Banana 2.1 and FLUX 3 Image comes from reviewers, API aggregators and developer blogs that repeat each other.
That matters for how much weight to put on any claim of leadership.
A model released 20 days ago has had little time for independent testing, and several of the headline numbers in this comparison come from the vendors themselves.
Google also keeps a higher tier.
Nano Banana Pro, built on Gemini 3 Pro Image, remains the heavier model, and the verified record shows no sign that Nano Banana 2.1 retired it.
Nano Banana 2.1 is an update to Nano Banana 2, which is Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, so it carries Flash-tier speed and price.
Where a spec is not in the verified record, the cell says so instead of guessing.
Read the table as a map of gaps as much as a spec sheet.
OpenAI does not publish a reference-image count in the notes I could verify, and Midjourney does not publish API specs because it has no API.
The Black Forest Labs row carries the largest uncertainty.
Third-party outlets report an October 1 launch for FLUX 3 Image, while an official BFL documentation page dated October 21 still describes the wider FLUX 3 family as early access.
Klein is the safer reference point because the October 15 press release confirms it.
Naming deserves its own warning.
OpenAI’s own materials use ChatGPT Images 2.5 for the consumer feature and GPT-Image-2.5 Flare and Sunburst for the API.
The phrase GPT Image 2.5 is shorthand that the press and search engines use, and no official standalone product carries that exact name.
Search for either form and you will find the right documents.
OpenAI released ChatGPT Images 2.5 and described it as its latest image-generation model.
The company says it improves detail, editing precision, reference-image preservation, multi-step instruction following, lighting and textures.
It also says generation latency fell by up to 50% compared with Images 2.0.
That last figure is vendor-measured, so treat it as a ceiling rather than a typical result.
For developers the launch split into two API models.
GPT-Image-2.5 Flare is the default choice for most applications.
GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst targets higher-precision creative work and takes longer per image.
The dated Sunburst snapshot is gpt-image-2.5-sunburst-2026-09-08, and pinning that snapshot keeps behavior stable between OpenAI updates.
OpenAI’s announcement says Images 2.5 is available on desktop, mobile and the web for all ChatGPT users, and it also covers ChatGPT Work and Codex.
Plan limits still apply, and the verified record does not spell out the free-tier allowance, so check your plan before you promise a client a volume of images.
On pricing, OpenAI lists Sunburst and Flare at $8 per 1 million image-input tokens, $2 per 1 million cached image-input tokens and $30 per 1 million image-output tokens.
Text input costs $5 per million tokens, or $1.25 cached.
Batch processing halves the image-output rate to $15 per million tokens.

OpenAI’s model page states that token rates match GPT Image 2, and one retrieved copy of OpenAI’s enterprise rate card still labels the line GPT-Image-2.0, a sign that the documentation lags the launch.
The weakness is predictability.
Because billing runs on tokens, one prompt can cost more than another depending on size, quality and how many reference images you attach.
OpenAI’s own calculator for GPT Image 2 does not estimate token use for 2.5.
A fair budgeting method is to run a pilot of 100 images with your real prompts, read the token counts from the API responses, and multiply.
Choosing between the two variants is mostly a question of what a wrong image costs you.
If a designer will review every output anyway, Flare’s faster turnaround keeps the loop tight and the bill lower.
If an image goes straight to a customer, such as a personalized product render or an ad variant, the extra seconds Sunburst needs can pay for themselves in fewer rejected results.
